## What peer review does

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Transactional

- Vets knowledge
- Routes work to stable material outcomes
- Maintains value of academic currency
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Discursive

- Gives authors feedback
- Sustains argument
- Builds community and mentors
:::
:::

### Where it happens

Journals, internal review, among friends and colleagues, open review platforms, blogs, journal clubs, hiring, grant review

::: {.notes}
Two kinds of work happen at once:

- Transactional functions:
  - Deciding to accept or reject knowledge claims
  - Producing stable and material research outcomes
  - Maintain the value of research papers, which serve as currency for hiring and promotion
- Discursive functions:
  - Give feedback
  - Sustain argument
  - Re-create disciplinary norms

Peer-review also occurs in settings other than journals:

- Internal institutional review
- Informal exchange among friends
- Open peer-review platforms (such as F1000 and PeerJ)
- Blogs and social media
- Journal clubs like this one
- Grant review
- Hiring
:::

## The three papers

| Paper | Source | Asks |
|--------------|--------------------|----------------------|
| Buriak et al. | ACS Nano editorial | What must stay human |
| Wu et al. | ACL survey | What AI can do |
| Pilatti et al. | Scoping review | Who stays accountable |

::: {.notes}
Three papers from three communities, so they carry different kinds of evidence.

**Buriak et al.**

- An editorial by journal editors, addressed to reviewers.
- It is a position piece, and its thesis is that peer review is a human responsibility that cannot be delegated to AI.
- It describes what makes a good review and which tasks LLMs cannot perform. That gives us a standard for assessing AI-assisted review.

**Wu et al.**

- This survey comes from the community that builds and evaluates AI reviewing systems, so it offers the technical perspective.
- It sets out how such systems are designed and how their output is assessed, and it identifies the problems that remain unresolved.

**Pilatti et al.**

- This scoping review examines how generative AI changes accountability in peer review, drawing on the research literature and institutional policies.
- It is about how to govern the use of AI in review so that reviewers remain accountable for their reports.
:::

## What a good review does

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026. Peer Review and AI: Your (Human) Opinion Is What Matters. ACS Nano.

:::

::: {.lines}
Produces a balanced report explaining the basis of the review

Recognizes the work's relevance to the broader field

Uses a constructive tone that supports improvement
:::

::: {.notes}
Before we ask what AI can do, we need a standard for what constitutes a good review. The factors below are drawn from Buriak et al. and serve as criteria against which AI-generated reviews can be assessed.

- The reviewer produces a balanced report that states the scientific value of the work, weighing its strengths and weaknesses.
- The review places the work in the broader field, assessing what distinguishes the work from existing work in the area.
- The tone is respectful and constructive, supporting authors' efforts to improve the work.
:::

## What LLMs can and cannot do

::: {.src}
Buriak et al. 2026, Figure 1.
:::

::: {.check}
| Task | LLM | Human |
|------------------------|--------|--------|
| Research summary | ✓ | ✓ |
| Grammar and spelling | ✓ | ✓ |
| Syntax | ✓ | ✓ |
| Inconsistencies | ✓ | ✓ |
| Novelty assessment | ✗ | ✓ |
| Critical thinking | ✗ | ✓ |
| Experimental logic | ✗ | ✓ |
| Data and graphics analysis | ✗ | ✓ |
:::

::: {.notes}
Buriak et al. sort the tasks of review into those an LLM can handle and those it cannot:

An LLM can handle the surface of review: summarizing the research, checking grammar, spelling, and syntax, and catching inconsistencies.

However, according to Buriak et al., it cannot assess novelty, think critically, evaluate the logic of the experiments, or analyze data and graphics.

These are their judgements, not test results, but similar claims were also asserted in last week's town hall about Hugo's work on AI peer-review.
:::

## Why AI is entering peer review

::: {.src}
Naddaf 2025. More than Half of Researchers Now Use AI for Peer Review — Often against Guidance. Nature.

:::

::: {.lines}
Submissions outgrow the pool of reviewers

Reviewing earns little credit

Reviewers already use AI, often against guidance
:::

::: {.notes}
LLMs are entering peer review despite these limits, because the system is under strain, specifically the fact that submissions are outpacing the pool of available reviewers, who are already extremely busy and who are not incentivized to review.

Use of AI is already widespread. A December 2025 survey, reported by _Nature_, suggests that more than half of researchers now use AI in peer review, often against guidance.
:::

## AI across the review pipeline

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026. Can AI Be a Good Peer Reviewer? A Survey of Peer Review Process, Evaluation, and the Future. ACL.
:::

::: {.flow}
<span class="step">Review</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Rebuttal</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Meta-review</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Decision</span><span class="arrow">→</span><span class="step">Revision</span>
:::

::: {.muted}
Methods for generating reviews
:::

::: {.chips}
<span class="chip">Fine-tuning</span><span class="chip">Multi-agent roles</span><span class="chip">Reinforcement learning</span><span class="chip">Retrieval and refinement</span>
:::

::: {.notes}
Given that pressure, researchers are building systems that assist or automate review. Wu et al. survey this work, and it spans the whole pipeline of review, rebuttal, meta-review, decision, and revision.

Most of the effort goes into the first stage, generating the review.

Prompting alone tends to produce generic and overly positive feedback, so researchers have developed four main approaches.

Some fine-tune models on expert reviews, some use multiple agents that each take a role such as novelty checking, some train with reinforcement learning against rewards for criticism, relevance, and actionable suggestions, and some retrieve related literature and refine the draft to ground its comments.

The later stages involve dialogue between authors and reviewers, and they have received far less attention than review generation.
:::

## Open problems in AI reviewing

::: {.src}
Wu et al. 2026.
:::

::: {.lines}
Novelty judgement remains weak

Review quality is hard to measure

Evidence comes almost entirely from NLP and ML

Rebuttal, meta-review, and revision are underexplored
:::

::: {.notes}
Even as these systems improve, Wu et al. identify four problems that remain open.

- One problem is novelty.
  - LLMs can imitate a reviewer's tone but remain weak at judging whether work is genuinely new.
  - Early systems write coherent critiques yet cannot distinguish incremental work from a breakthrough without broader scientific context, and benchmarks built to test novelty assessment show how difficult this remains.

- Another is measuring review quality, which matters because any claim that AI review is good enough depends on how quality is measured.
  - The common approach scores a generated review by its overlap with human-written reviews.
  - That rewards surface similarity and says little about correctness or constructiveness. Some datasets are starting to be developed to reach beyond this limitation.

- A third is the evidence base.
  - Most peer review datasets come from NLP and ML conferences, which limits how far the findings generalize.
  - Wu et al. note that broader coverage is needed to test whether current models overfit to domain-specific language.

- The last concerns the steps after the review.
  - Rebuttal, meta-review, and revision involve richer argument and collaboration between authors and reviewers, yet benchmarks for them are sparse.
:::

## AI-assisted review is a governance problem

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026. AI-Assisted Peer Review: A Scoping Review of Governance, Ethical-Behavioral Risks, and Integrity. Ethics & Behavior.
:::

::: {.lines}
Prohibition and detection alone will not contain AI use

Governance has to make judgement verifiable
:::

| Risk | What goes wrong |
|------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Accountability laundering | A signed report vouches for unchecked work |
| AI reports that evade detection | Bans fail, and hidden use exposes manuscripts |
| Prompt injection | Hidden instructions steer reviewers' AI tools |

::: {.notes}
Wu et al. survey AI systems built to generate the review, and Pilatti et al. ask how the governance of peer review has to change once those systems are in use.

Pilatti's scoping review treats AI-assisted review as a problem of institutional governance that goes beyond individual conduct. Prohibition and detection cannot stop reviewers from using AI, because that use is hard to see, so they argue that governance has to make judgement verifiable.

The authors identify a few significant risks:

- Reviewers may outsource the central steps of a review to AI, which leads to accountability laundering, in which a report still carries a named reviewer's endorsement although no one checked the work behind it.
- AI-generated reports are also hard to detect, so rules against AI use are hard to enforce.
- Furthermore, reviewers who use AI out of sight tend to rely on external tools, which breaches confidentiality.
- Finally, authors have injected prompts in manuscripts to manipulate the AI tools that reviewers use.
:::

## Making judgement verifiable

::: {.src}
Pilatti et al. 2026.
:::

| Risk | Response |
|------------------------|------------------------------------|
| Accountability laundering | Reviewers verify; journals audit a sample |
| AI reports that evade detection | Reviewers disclose AI use; journals control the tools |
| Prompt injection | Journals sanitize manuscripts before AI processing |

::: {.notes}
Pilatti et al. conclude that peer review stays a practice of responsible judgement only if AI-assisted work becomes more verifiable. For each of the three risks, they propose responses that reviewers and institutions can carry out and check.

- To counter accountability laundering, Pilatti et al. suggest treating AI output as a suggestion only.
  - The reviewer checks each suggestion against the manuscript and answers for every claim in the report, including claims the tool raised first.
  - The journal then audits a sample of reports, asking whether the comments point to specific sections, figures, or tables, whether strong recommendations are justified, and whether any claims cannot be verified.

- For reports that evade detection, Pilatti et al. propose requiring specific disclosure of the task AI performed, whether manuscript content was processed and under what conditions, and whether the tool transformed the report beyond language polishing.
  - They argue that this gives reviewers a regulated path for uses that are likely to happen anyway, which reduces the incentive to conceal them, but they list whether it works as a hypothesis to test.
  - AI used on a manuscript should preferably run in an environment controlled by the journal or another institution, with guarantees that the manuscript is not retained or used for training.
  - More robust regimes have journals offer internal tools, with access logs for later investigation.

- For prompt injection, manuscripts are sanitized before any AI processing.
  - That means removing invisible text, normalizing formatting, and flagging suspicious elements, which reduces the attack surface.

- Effort shifts from writing reviews to checking them.
  - The reviewer checks the tool, and the journal checks the reviews.
  - Pilatti et al. add that reducing workload cannot mean reducing responsibility.
:::

## Discussion

1. Who is peer review for?
2. How should review work be divided between AI and the reviewer?
3. Is resemblance to human reviews the right test of an AI review's quality?
4. Do authors take criticism from an AI differently than from a peer?
5. Who is accountable for reasoning the reviewer did not produce?

::: {.notes}
1. Buriak et al. say reviewers provide a critical, essential service to the scientific community, and that good reviews help authors improve and support a robust literature and trainee education. Pilatti et al. describe review as a pact of trust that links competence, confidentiality, and accountability to editorial decisions and the credibility of the scientific record. Each answer implies something different about what is worth automating.

2. Buriak et al. separate what an LLM can do from what it may be used for. An LLM can summarize the research, check grammar, spelling, and syntax, and catch inconsistencies. It cannot assess novelty, think critically, judge the logic of experiments, or analyze data and figures. Buriak et al. also prohibit uploading a manuscript to an LLM for review, and they do not support using one even to check a draft of a reviewer report. Pilatti et al. draw the line by risk. They count language editing of the reviewer's own report as a low-exposure use, and they treat summarizing the manuscript, listing limitations, and drafting recommendations as the central steps that are easiest to outsource. Their rule is that the system should relieve mechanical tasks and leave the judgement with the reviewer.

3. Wu et al.'s reference-based evaluation assumes that a better AI review overlaps more with human-written reviews. They say such metrics often capture lexical or semantic overlap more than scientific validity, reasoning quality, or constructiveness, and can penalize valid feedback that is phrased differently. Human reviews are also imperfect. Buriak et al. cite unchecked bias, conflicts of interest, and gatekeeping, and Pilatti et al. cite a study finding that citations and self-citations influence reviews. The question is whether resemblance to human reviews is the right test of an AI review's quality.

4. Buriak et al. say generic, formulaic AI-generated reviews can leave authors discouraged, disillusioned, and frustrated, and they note that manuscripts often include students for whom this is a first exposure to peer review. In a user study cited by Wu et al., 308 researchers received LLM-generated feedback on their own papers and perceived it as valuable. None of the three papers compares how authors react to AI feedback and to peer feedback, so this question goes beyond them.

5. Pilatti et al. place accountability with the reviewer, who must be able to answer for every substantive claim in the report, including claims a tool suggested first. Buriak et al. add that a computer cannot be held accountable. How anyone would know is the harder part. Pilatti et al. propose that journals audit a sample of reports for comments anchored in the manuscript, and that reviewers disclose how they used AI.
:::
